glossary.definition: The total global or regional market demand for a product or service, calculated as the maximum possible annual revenue if the company captured 100% market share.
glossary.formula: TAM = Total Target Accounts in World × Average Annual Contract Value (ACV)

glossary.definition: The specific segment of the Total Addressable Market that a company can realistically target and serve given its current geography, channel capabilities, and product specialization.
glossary.formula: SAM = Target Accounts within Reachable Geography/Channel × ACV

glossary.definition: The portion of the Serviceable Addressable Market that a company expects to realistically capture within the next 12 to 36 months, factoring in competition and sales bandwidth.
glossary.formula: SOM = SAM × Realistic Market Share Percentage (typically 1% - 5%)

glossary.definition: The total financial outlay required to acquire a single new paying customer, factoring in all sales salaries, ad spend, creative agency fees, and marketing software.
glossary.formula: CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Costs in Period / New Customers Acquired in Period

glossary.definition: The total net gross profit that an individual customer will generate for a business over the entire duration of their commercial relationship.
glossary.formula: LTV = (Average Revenue Per User × Gross Margin %) / Churn Rate

glossary.definition: A golden benchmark ratio measuring the return on marketing capital. A ratio of 3:1 is considered healthy; below 1:1 loses money on each customer, while above 5:1 suggests underinvestment in marketing.
glossary.formula: LTV:CAC = Customer Lifetime Value / Customer Acquisition Cost

glossary.definition: The predictable, normalized revenue stream a subscription business collects every 30 days. Excludes one-off setup fees and non-recurring consulting revenue.
glossary.formula: MRR = Total Paying Subscribers × Average Monthly Subscription Price

glossary.definition: The annualized value of recurring subscription revenue. The standard valuation multiple metric for venture-scale B2B SaaS businesses.
glossary.formula: ARR = MRR × 12

glossary.definition: The number of months required for a company to earn back the capital spent acquiring a customer from that customer's gross profit contribution.
glossary.formula: Payback Months = CAC / (Monthly ARPU × Gross Margin %)

glossary.definition: The percentage rate at which customers cancel their subscriptions or recurring revenue is lost within a specified time interval (typically monthly or annually).
glossary.formula: Monthly Customer Churn = (Customers Lost in Month / Customers at Start of Month) × 100

glossary.definition: The percentage of recurring revenue retained from an existing cohort of customers over a period, accounting for upgrades, downgrades, and cancellations. NRR > 100% means the cohort grows without new customer acquisition.
glossary.formula: NRR = [(Starting ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Starting ARR] × 100

glossary.definition: The percentage of revenue retained after deducting the direct cost of goods sold (COGS) or hosting, customer support, and third-party APIs needed to deliver the service.
glossary.formula: Gross Margin % = [(Revenue - COGS) / Revenue] × 100

glossary.definition: Revenue remaining per unit after deducting variable costs. It indicates how much each sale contributes to covering fixed overhead expenses like office rent and executive salaries.
glossary.formula: Contribution Margin per Unit = Selling Price per Unit - Variable Cost per Unit

glossary.definition: The rate at which a company expends cash. Gross burn is total monthly cash spent; Net burn is cash spent minus incoming cash collections.
glossary.formula: Net Monthly Burn = Gross Operating Expenses - Collected Revenue

glossary.definition: The amount of time in months a company has before it exhausts its cash reserves, assuming current net monthly burn remains constant.
glossary.formula: Runway (Months) = Current Liquid Cash Balance / Net Monthly Burn

glossary.definition: A capital efficiency metric coined by Craft Ventures that measures how much cash a startup burns to generate each dollar of Net New ARR.
glossary.formula: Burn Multiple = Net Burn in Period / Net New ARR Added in Period

glossary.definition: A benchmark for software businesses stating that the combined sum of year-over-year revenue growth rate percentage and profit margin percentage should equal or exceed 40%.
glossary.formula: Rule of 40 Score = Annual Revenue Growth Rate % + Free Cash Flow (or EBITDA) Margin %

glossary.definition: The inflection point where a product satisfies strong commercial demand in a sizable market, evidenced by sustained retention cohorts, organic word of mouth, and accelerating inbound sales.
glossary.formula: Sean Ellis Benchmark: ≥ 40% of surveyed users report they would be 'very disappointed' without the product

glossary.definition: The simplest version of a product that can be released to early adopters to validate core hypotheses and gather feedback with minimal engineering investment.
A categorical description of the perfect company or buyer account that derives the highest value from your product, experiences the lowest churn, and has the shortest sales cycle.
A go-to-market business methodology in which user acquisition, onboarding, retention, and expansion are primarily driven by the product itself rather than direct sales reps.
glossary.example_or_formula: Example companies: Slack, Notion, Zoom, Figma

glossary.definition: A go-to-market model where qualified enterprise pipeline generation, custom demo presentations, contract negotiations, and procurement reviews are driven by sales executives.
glossary.example_or_formula: Common for ACV > $25,000 where security compliance, SSO, and customized terms are mandatory

glossary.definition: A pricing strategy where basic functionality is provided free of charge to maximize top-of-funnel adoption, while advanced features, higher capacity, or team collaboration are paywalled.
The process of building and scaling a company solely using personal savings, sweat equity, and customer revenues without taking institutional venture capital.
A framework coined by Paul Graham. A company is 'Default Alive' if its current revenue growth rate will carry it to profitability before its remaining cash runs out without raising more capital.
glossary.formula: Default Alive = Projected Cash Balance at Breakeven Point > $0

glossary.definition: A standardized legal instrument created by Y Combinator allowing investors to provide early cash in exchange for the contractual right to receive equity in a future priced round.
A debt instrument that carries an interest rate and maturity date, which automatically converts into preferred stock when the startup closes a qualified priced equity round.
The maximum effective enterprise valuation at which an early investor's convertible instrument (SAFE or Convertible Note) will convert into equity, protecting them from excessive dilution.
Pre-money valuation is the agreed value of the company before receiving new investment cash. Post-money is the valuation immediately following the investment.
glossary.formula: Post-Money Valuation = Pre-Money Valuation + New Investment Capital

glossary.definition: A detailed mathematical ledger listing all founders, angel investors, venture funds, and option pool holders along with their ownership percentages, equity classes, and share counts.
The decrease in an existing shareholder's percentage ownership of a company that occurs whenever new shares of stock are issued to incoming investors or an employee option pool.
glossary.formula: New Ownership % = Existing Shares / (Total Existing Shares + Newly Issued Shares)

glossary.definition: A schedule by which founders and employees earn equity over time (typically 4 years with a 1-year cliff). If an individual leaves before 12 months, they forfeit 100% of their equity grant.
A non-binding summary agreement laying out the core financial and legal terms under which a venture capital firm will invest in a company (valuation, board seats, liquidation preferences).
The investment fund or angel that writes the largest check in a financing round, negotiates the terms of the term sheet, and frequently takes a seat on the board of directors.
The number of new users an existing user successfully recruits into the product. A K-factor greater than 1.0 represents exponential, self-sustaining viral growth.
glossary.formula: K = Number of Invites Sent per User × Conversion Rate of Invitees

glossary.definition: A business model dynamic where each component of the business feeds positive momentum into the next step, causing the overall system to accelerate with decreasing incremental friction.
glossary.example_or_formula: Amazon Flywheel: Lower Prices → More Customers → More Third-Party Sellers → Economies of Scale → Lower Prices

glossary.definition: A distinct, sustainable competitive advantage that prevents competitors from easily copying a company's product, stealing customers, or eroding its operating profit margins.
The total friction—financial, operational, psychological, or time-related—incurred by a customer if they decide to switch from your product to a competitor's solution.
The phenomenon where a product or platform becomes exponentially more valuable to every existing user as additional users join the network.
A structured course correction designed to test a new fundamental hypothesis about the product, customer segment, or business model while maintaining the company's core vision.
The analytical practice of grouping users by their join date (e.g., January 2026 cohort) to track their retention, engagement, and spending patterns over time independently of new sign-ups.
A lean validation tactic where a landing page or advertisement for a non-existent product is launched to measure customer intent through click-through rates, pre-orders, or sign-ups.
A formal non-binding document signed by an enterprise buyer expressing their intent to purchase and implement a product once specific technical features and milestones are completed.
A concept popularized by Peter Thiel describing the act of creating something genuinely novel and transformative, as opposed to copying existing models (going from 1 to n).
The average monthly or annual revenue generated per active subscriber or user account across the entire paying customer base.
glossary.formula: ARPU = Total Collected Revenue in Month / Total Active Paying Accounts in Month
